title: More isn't more (Avot 2:7)
hookLine: more flesh, more worms; more possessions, more worry; more Torah, more life

cards: The shoes, the gadget, the bigger apartment: the thing someone really wanted, finally bought. For a few days, it was wonderful. Then, quietly, it came with things.
A password to remember. A warranty to register. A thing to insure, to clean, to worry about scratching.
A rented storage unit is a monument to this feeling. Hillel noticed it too, and turned it into a saying with a beat. It sounds almost like a chant.

teach.b: Here's how his list begins. More flesh, more worms.
More possessions, more worry. It's blunt. A body fattened on luxury ends in the same grave as everyone else's, and the more you own, the more you have to guard.
In Hebrew it has a beat: marbeh nekhasim, marbeh de'agah.
The list goes on through the households of his ancient world, with a few lines about servants and wives that read uncomfortably today, and are honestly part of the text. Then the list turns.

teach.h: THE LIST TURNS: MORE TORAH, MORE LIFE.
teach.b: More Torah, more life. More sitting in study, more wisdom. More counsel, more understanding.
More tzedakah, giving to those in need, more peace. Hillel isn't against more. Some kinds of more shrink you, and some kinds grow you.
Possessions pile up and need guarding. Wisdom, understanding and generosity pile up and set you free. And the surprise: giving looks like it should leave a person with less.

Hillel says it leaves you with more peace. Then one more line: a person who has gained a good name has gained it for himself, but a person who has gained words of Torah has gained life in the world to come.
A good name is precious, he seems to say, but it stays here. What you learn and give goes further.
More isn't more. The question is always: more of what?

how: Giving tzedakah, charity understood as justice, is a central Jewish practice, and some households keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat.

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: Hillel is against having more of anything
he names kinds of more that grow you: Torah, wisdom, counsel, giving.
Hillel says more giving brings more peace
more tzedakah, more peace, near the end of his list.
the whole list sounds modern today
a few lines about servants and wives reflect his ancient world and read uncomfortably now.

games.q: you've just gotten a raise. what would Hillel's list suggest you get more of?
o: more things, and a bigger place to keep them.
more savings, and worry about them.
games.why: more possessions, more worry; but more Torah, more life, and more tzedakah, more peace.

practice: Picture walking slowly through your home, a closet, a drawer, a shelf, and find one thing you keep but don't need that someone else could use: a coat, a book, a pan. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it.
Then picture it in someone else's hands, being useful, and see if the tug loosens.

wordCard.voice: Marbeh de'agah. More possessions, more worry: the beat of Hillel's list, before it turns to more learning, more life, and more giving, more peace.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: more possessions, more worry.

carryVoice: Your line: more giving, more peace. The whole list runs on one word, marbeh. Day two hundred fifty-six.
